original_relations.description: Both are autoregressive neural construction policies; AM replaces the recurrent Pointer Network stack with multi-head attention.
Both learn sequential construction policies, while VRP-RL extends the formulation with dynamic state for vehicle-routing decisions.
Both train constructive TSP policies with policy gradients; Learning Heuristic uses an attention-only design and can pair it with 2-opt.
Both learn constructive heuristics with reinforcement learning, using a sequence Pointer Network and graph embeddings with Q-learning respectively.
Both construct vehicle routes autoregressively, with different representations, decoder contexts, and reinforcement-learning baselines.
AM-D revisits attention-based routing by recomputing representations as the vehicle-routing state changes instead of relying only on static encodings.
Both use attention and pointer-style autoregressive routing; GPN/HGPN adds relative graph context and a hierarchical formulation.
Both construct VRP solutions, while GCN-NPEC combines node-edge graph convolutions with an auxiliary edge-classification objective.
These contemporaneous attention-only TSP policies differ in decoder context, training baselines, and their use of optional local search.
Both encode graph structure for TSP, using Q-learning for greedy construction and supervised edge heatmaps for beam search respectively.
Both use edge-aware graph convolutions and explicit edge predictions, for TSP heatmaps and joint VRP decoding respectively.
Both update the representation used by an autoregressive policy as the partially constructed route and remaining choices evolve.
Both study graph-based reinforcement-learning heuristics and generalization, with different policy and value formulations.
Both use Transformer-style routing representations, but one constructs a route and the other learns iterative pairwise improvements.
Both learn edge-level guidance that is consumed by a downstream combinatorial search procedure rather than returned as a final solution directly.
Both place learned guidance inside an iterative search process, using learned pair moves and ant-colony search with local search respectively.
The methods connect policy-gradient VRP learning with a later joint reinforcement and supervised edge-classification training objective.
Both use attention-based construction, while GOAL shares a backbone across problem types through lightweight task-specific adapters.
Both cover multiple combinatorial problem families, contrasting per-problem learned ACO guidance with a shared multi-task backbone.
PN-AC adopts the Pointer Network mechanism as an autoregressive policy and changes the learning signal from supervised targets to reinforcement learning.
Both point to input nodes during construction; AM replaces recurrent encoding with a Transformer-style attention stack.
Both repeatedly rewrite an incumbent solution with learned local decisions, using different state encoders and neighborhood definitions.
Both separate a feasible incumbent from a learned policy that chooses iterative local modifications.
NeuRewriter provides a general local-rewrite abstraction, whereas Neural-3-OPT specializes the learned action to three-edge TSP reconnections.
Sym-NCO extends POMO-style training with explicit regularizers for problem and solution symmetries.
P-MOCO conditions a POMO-style constructive policy on objective preferences so one model can sample an approximate Pareto set.
SGBS uses pretrained POMO policies as search guidance and adds rollout-ranked beam expansion at inference time.
Both train constructive routing policies with policy gradients; DRO changes the training distribution through a robust minimax objective.
Both learn graph representations for sequential TSP decisions, pairing them with MCTS priors and Q-learning respectively.
Both use complete rollouts to assess partial tours, with MCTS maintaining a search tree and SGBS retaining a fixed-width beam.
Both combine learned edge guidance with an external search process to avoid returning a purely greedy neural tour.
Both improve CVRP incumbents iteratively, contrasting learned large-neighborhood repair with edge-aware local move selection.
Both start from feasible vehicle routes and learn repeated improvement, using destroy-repair and a portfolio of local operators respectively.
Both solve selected routing subproblems inside a larger loop; L2D learns which spatial subproblem to send to an interchangeable solver.
Both encode the incumbent CVRP solution and learn a policy over feasible local modifications.
Both target vehicle-routing improvement, while RBG organizes decisions hierarchically for much larger logistics instances.
Both use reinforcement learning to sequence local routing moves and retain the best incumbent over an iteration budget.
MDAM shares an attention encoder across several diverse decoders rather than relying on AM's single decoding policy.
Both generate diverse candidate routes before selecting or revising the best, using decoder diversity and collaborative seeding respectively.
Both extend attention-based construction with specialized representation modules, for diverse routing modes and matrix-valued problem data.
MatNet adapts attention encoding to rectangular relation matrices while retaining an autoregressive construction pipeline.
Both build POMO-style end-to-end policies on specialized encoders, for matrix problems and preference-conditioned multi-objective routing.
Both learn iterative tour improvement; Neural-3-OPT selects three removed edges and a reconnection while DACT learns pairwise transformations.
Both use learned attention to choose local tour edits, with different three-edge and pairwise neighborhoods.
Both predict edge-level TSP guidance with graph networks, consumed by LKH candidate search and beam search respectively.
Both reuse neural edge predictions inside a classical or structured search procedure to scale beyond direct decoding.
Both guide established TSP improvement heuristics with learned edge signals, targeting LKH candidates and GLS penalties respectively.
Both combine learned graph guidance with a non-neural combinatorial engine and expose explicit search budgets at inference.
Both learn edge heatmaps with graph convolutions, differing in their decomposition and downstream tour-merging search.
Both avoid a single autoregressive tour and use learned edge distributions to support scalable candidate search.
Both improve large routing solutions through learned subproblem decisions, using neural sub-tour revision and black-box delegation.
Both use hierarchical policies to divide global exploration from lower-level route refinement.
Both target large logistics routing through spatial decomposition, with learned delegation and hierarchical region construction.
Both decompose larger routing decisions hierarchically, but L2D delegates local subproblems to an external solver.
Both learn a distribution that is searched at inference time rather than treating a single network output as the final solution.
Both optimize a continuous generative representation before decoding or discretizing it into a routing solution.
Both adapt a compact set of variables for each target instance instead of retraining all policy parameters.
Both use attention-based autoregressive construction; Step-Wise recomputes embeddings after each routing decision.
Both make routing representations dynamic as the partial solution evolves, through full step-wise encoding and dynamic attention updates.
Both encode changing vehicle state during construction, for a single route context and cooperative multi-vehicle agents respectively.

Both learn attention-based policies for repeated pairwise routing improvements; DACT replaces LIH's single-stream representation and recurrent search signal with dual node-position streams and cyclic positional encoding.
Both learn which parts of a current tour deserve modification, coupled with neural moves and Guided Local Search.
Both learn edge-level solution distributions for TSP; DIMES makes the distribution a continuous target for parallel fine-tuning.
Both search continuous probabilistic representations before producing discrete tours, using meta-learned logits and diffusion priors.
Both use learned edge guidance to explore many discrete candidates rather than greedily decoding one route.
SGBS and EAS are explicitly combined: rollout-ranked beam search improves samples used for lightweight test-time adaptation.
DPDP consumes learned edge heatmaps in a dominance-aware dynamic-programming beam rather than ordinary sequence beam search.
Both learn edge-aware VRP guidance, used for restricted dynamic programming and joint autoregressive construction respectively.
Sym-NCO can regularize an AM backbone so equivalent transformed routing instances produce consistent representations and solutions.
Both extend POMO-style policy optimization with additional structure, using symmetry consistency and objective preferences.
Both improve distribution generalization through training-time objectives, emphasizing geometric symmetry and worst-case data shifts.
Both condition routing decisions on dynamic vehicle state; MAPDP distributes decisions across cooperating vehicle agents.
Both address logistics routing with multiple decision makers or regions, at cooperative pickup-delivery and large-scale hierarchical levels.
Both represent TSP solutions through soft edge structures, followed by iterative guided denoising and beam/local search respectively.
Both predict edge signals with graph networks and hand them to downstream TSP search instead of decoding a final route directly.
Both optimize routing policies from task rewards; EAS restricts gradient updates to lightweight parameters for one test instance.
DRO uses graph-based routing components while changing training toward worst-case instance distributions rather than nominal sampling alone.
LEHD and AM are autoregressive attention solvers; LEHD moves most relational modeling into a heavier dynamic decoder to improve scale transfer.
BQ-NCO and AM construct routes sequentially, while BQ-NCO compresses decision-equivalent states before scoring the remaining actions.
Both use diffusion to refine soft combinatorial structure, with DIFUSCO learning a graph-conditioned reverse process and DMPP supplying a plug-and-play prior.
Both optimize continuous noisy solution representations before discrete decoding; T2T emphasizes objective-gradient search at test time.
NeuOpt and DACT learn iterative routing improvements, using flexible k-opt moves across feasible and infeasible regions and paired node actions respectively.
Both apply learned policies repeatedly to improve incumbent routes; NCS coordinates multiple complementary policies for pickup-and-delivery neighborhoods.

Both study graph-based TSP prediction, with Less Is More isolating candidate-graph sparsity as a central representation choice.
COMPASS and EAS adapt a pretrained solver to a target instance, searching a latent policy code and updating lightweight active-search parameters respectively.

TAM and GPN/HGPN transfer small routing policies to larger instances through learned high-level decomposition and local construction.
Pointerformer retains attention-based autoregressive construction while adding reversible encoding and a multi-pointer decoder for larger TSPs.
ReLD revisits the AM-style encoder-decoder balance and preserves selected dynamic context in a much lighter sequential decoder.
Both adapt neural solvers after pretraining; Meta-SAGE meta-learns a cross-scale adaptation schedule while EAS optimizes a small parameter subset per instance.

Both seek broad coverage, with Omni-VRP targeting compound routing shifts and GOAL sharing a backbone across distinct combinatorial problem families.
